b: These days, Tony Van Horn’s life is consumed by “the streak.”
In spring, the Pennsylvania fisherman set out to see how many consecutive days he could catch a fish. And as Thanksgiving nears, that streak continues.
As of Nov. 18, he had fished for 239 days in a row and caught more than 1,165 smallmouth bass.
Along the way, he fished in blistering heat, high water, drought conditions, rain, sleet, and numbing cold.
But he has yet to get skunked.
“As long as it’s not lightning, I’ll fish in every type of weather, all the way down to sub-zero temperatures,” Van Horn told Wired2fish. “I’m out there year-round.”
Understand that Van Horn is not some high-profile pro fisherman. He is just an average guy who has an above-average passion for fishing.

He lives in Oil City, a small town in northwestern Pennsylvania surrounded by water and fishing opportunities. He can walk 200 yards from his home to the banks of the Allegheny River, where he does most of his fishing in the spring and fall months.

“My stretch of the Allegheny is on the inside of a bend, so I have an eddy and a couple little troughs that hold fish,” said 35-year-old Van Horn. “There are lots of smallmouth in there, and I have my favorite spots where I can usually catch them.”
In the summer, he shifts his focus to Oil Creek, a tributary of the Allegheny, which has waterfalls and rapids to oxygenate the water.
Between those two spots, he knows he always has a shot at catching smallmouth.
“I’ve been able to catch smallmouth every day of my streak, except for four days,” he said. “Three of those times I caught trout, which my buddy (Brandon Melat) and I were targeting.
“The other day, a big storm hit and turned the rivers to chocolate milk, so I fished a farm pond and caught 15 to 20 largemouth bass.”
Some fishermen dream of fishing every day, but few make that a reality like Tony Van Horn does. Photo by Tony Van Horn.
Van Horn isn’t a trophy hunter. He doesn’t carry a scale or even a ruler. He isn’t looking for a fish for the wall.

But that doesn’t mean he doesn’t catch some big smallmouth. He estimates that his biggest fish weighed 4.5 pounds. And he regularly catches fish that he estimates in the 1.5- to two-pound range in the spring and fall.
All smallmouths are considered equal in his eyes. He catches them, usually takes a selfie, then releases them.
His trips usually aren’t long. He fishes when he has time, and a lot of days, that amounts to an hour or two. He often fishes from the bank or by wading.
He works long hours at a factory job. And once fall arrives, he is often out hunting with his dad.
He has already taken his buck this year, and he and his dad have enjoyed several days following their bird dog in pursuit of pheasants.
But there is always time for fishing — and keeping the streak alive.
“Sometimes, I might only have an hour to fish,” Van Horn said. “The longest it has taken me was three hours, and that was after a 10-hour day at work.
“It was hot and I was exhausted. But I had to keep the streak going.”
Van Horn considers himself lucky to live in northwestern Pennsylvania, where the fishing and hunting opportunities are abundant.
He grew up fishing Oil Creek and the Allegheny River, usually with his best friend Brandon Melat. The two are still close, and fish together whenever possible.
They fish the nearby smallmouth waters and travel to central Pennsylvania to fish for brook and brown trout on the streams there.

In the harsh winter months, they get together to make soft plastic baits for their own use. And they also sell those baits through their MVB (Most Valuable Baits) company. In fact, the duo plans to expand the small business in the near future.
Van Horn can certainly provide authentic, firsthand marketing for the baits’ effectiveness. Each of the smallmouth he has caught during his streak came on one of the MVB homemade baits.
“Swimbaits are my absolute favorite,” Van Horn said. “But I’ve caught smallmouth on a lot of our baits — paddletails, small craws, even some of our smaller baits for panfish and trout.”
As for his streak? Van Horn senses it will end soon with the time change and the advance of winter, when the smallmouth become harder to catch.
“I like to fish for walleyes in the fall, but they’re not a sure thing,” Van Horn said. “Even if it ends, I won’t have any regrets.
“The overall experience is what counts, and I’ll remember this for a long time.”
About the lead image: Tony Van Horn of Oil City, Pennsylvania, has a knack for catching smallmouth bass, and he has an impressive streak to prove it. Photo by Tony Van Horn.
